messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Assuming “Majid” and “Majeed” refer to the same character, the quoted lines do not show his usual cunning and apathy in a fully obvious way. They show urgency, physical effort, and control. He wakes the others, takes charge, carries Jamila, and moves them toward the village. The detail of the “thin quilt” suggests he is at least attending to their exposure and vulnerability, which complicates a simple reading of him as apathetic. The “brilliant moonlight” blinding him also humanizes him; he is momentarily disoriented, not a cold, omniscient manipulator.

However, the tone is still directive rather than tender: “Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village.” The command frames Rahima and Jamila as people to be managed, not as persons whose moral worth is being celebrated. If Majeed has been portrayed as cunning and apathetic, this scene can be read as those traits wearing a practical mask. His action may not be pure warmth; it may be a strategic response to danger, social expectation, or self-interest. He may be moving them to the village because it avoids harm, preserves order, protects his reputation, or keeps them under his control. In that sense, apathy is less visible here, but calculation remains plausible.

On the deontology/teleology question, the lines support a **teleological** reading more than a **deontological** one. A deontological motive would mean he acts because it is intrinsically right, or because duty requires it, regardless of consequences. The passage does not show him appealing to moral law, conscience, or obligation for its own sake. Instead, it shows him stating a goal: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” That is outcome-oriented. The action is justified by what it produces: movement to safety, shelter, continuation, or avoidance of worse consequences. If his character has been self-interested, the most likely explanation is that this is a well-calculated protective move: he saves or moves them because the consequences of not doing so are worse, or because his interests are tied to theirs. It may resemble duty, but the available textual evidence points to pragmatic calculation rather than pure goodwill.

Required single-word palindromes, each at least five characters: kayak, level, radar, civic, refer, rotor, madam, tenet, deified, reviver.
